name: The Japanese Maple of Waldeckpark
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (LRMB v2024), Bomenstichting, register nr 1678456: 'Japanse esdoorn', Waldeckpark, planted band 1910-1920, owner_category gemeente, setting park, visitable ja

https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldeckpark (confirms Waldeckpark was laid out in 1921 by Leonard Springer on the former Bastion Waldeck, is a public municipal park with monumental trees, though does not name this specific specimen)
access: Free. Stands in Waldeckpark on Prins Bisschopsingel, a municipally owned public park; open at all times like any city park.
transport: Short walk from Maastricht city centre and from the other Waldeckpark/Aldenhofpark trees already published (maa_012, maa_013, maa_014); the busy Prins Bisschopsingel road separates it from the adjoining Stadspark, so cross at the signalled crossing.
story:
The national register puts this Japanese maple in the planting years 1910 to 1920. The park around it was laid out in 1921. Both statements come from good sources and nobody has reconciled them: either the maple was already standing on the old Bastion Waldeck before Leonard Springer drew his park over the demolished fortification, or the register's decade band is simply loose. Worth knowing, and not yet written down anywhere.

What the band does give is a bracket of roughly 106 to 116 years, which is a long life for Acer palmatum. The species is a slow, small tree, planted across Europe since the nineteenth century as a garden ornament and rarely allowed to get old; most of the Japanese maples anyone has met are shrubs you can see over the top of. This one has had a century in municipal ground, which is why the register marks it as dendrologically notable rather than merely present.

It is also, so far, a tree only one source names. Waldeckpark and the Stadspark it adjoins hold more than 800 trees between them across some 160 species, and the histories of the park describe that collection without singling this specimen out. It stands with the park's Caucasian wingnut, golden rain tree and sweet gum, four trees in a few minutes of walking.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the small palm-shaped leaves, cut into five to seven narrow lobes and scarlet in October, on a low tree rather than one of the park's tall ones. It stands in Waldeckpark, off Prins Bisschopsingel.

best_time.label: October and November, when the leaves run from orange into deep red

name: The Plane Tree of Sint-Servaasbron
verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (LRMB v2024), Bomenstichting, register nr 1691040: 'Gewone plataan St.Servaasbron', Cannerweg 451, planted band 1900-1910, owner_category religieuze instantie, setting bos, visitable ja, visible ja

https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sint-Servaasbron (confirms the site's legend, that the current stone well dates to 1886-88, that it is surrounded by chestnut trees and elder bushes, that it is a protected national monument reached through a decorative Louis XV-style gate, and that an annual May procession is still held there); corroborated by https://rijksmonumenten.nl/monument/27941/st-servatiusbron/maastricht/ (national monument listing) and https://www.bronnen-krachtplaatsen.info/li-maastricht-sint-servaas-bron.php (recent visitor account confirming public access via a small stairway to the well)
access: Free and open. The grounds around the spring belong to a religious institution per the register, but the site is a national monument (rijksmonument) reached through an unlocked decorative gate, visited by the public year-round, and hosts a public procession every May; the register itself marks the tree 'visitable: ja'.
transport: In the Jekerdal valley off the Cannerweg, on the city's south-west edge near the Belgian border; about 1.6 km (roughly 20 minutes on foot along the Cannerweg/Jekerpad) from the already-published 1700 Oaks of Cannerbos (maa_003).
story:
The legend, recorded in the Middle Ages by Henric van Veldeke, has Saint Servatius striking the ground here with his staff on his way home from Rome, and a spring rising where it landed. A woman with a fever was said to have been cured by the water. People have been coming down to it ever since, and a procession still walks here every May.

What you actually find at the bottom of the little stairway is nineteenth-century: a stone well under a wrought-iron canopy with a statue of the saint above it, built between 1886 and 1888 and now a national monument in its own right. The plane standing over it is dated by the national register to the planting years 1900 to 1910, roughly 120 years, so tree and stonework are near contemporaries. Whether the tree went in as part of that work, nobody recorded.

The ground belongs to a religious institution, but the gate is a decorative Louis XV affair that stands unlocked, the register marks the tree as visitable, and the site is walked by the public year round. The spring itself is less reliable than the tree: a recent visitor account found it dry.

The plane has company. Chestnuts and elder crowd the hollow, and the register lists a grove of 23 maples and horse chestnuts at the same coordinates, dated 1860 to 1870. Only the plane carries a name.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one plane among the chestnuts and elder around the spring, its bark flaking into cream and olive patches. It stands over the stone well at the foot of the stairway, off the Cannerweg.

name: The Plane Trees of Mgr. Nolenspark

location.address: Monseigneur Nolenspark, along Van Heylerhofflaan, Maastricht

verified_sources: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen (LRMB v2024), Bomenstichting, register nr 1696504: 'Platanengroep Mgr.Nolenspark Maastricht', 3 trees, planted band 1880-1890, owner_category gemeente, setting park, visitable ja, visible ja

https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldeckpark and general Stadspark history (independently confirms Mgr. Nolenspark was added to the Stadspark complex from 1886 to a design by (the younger) Rosseels, matching the register's own history note that the planes 'presumably date from this period')
access: Free. Stands in the municipally owned Mgr. Nolenspark, part of Maastricht's public Stadspark system, open at all times.
transport: Same small cluster as the already-published Black Walnuts (maa_008), Weeping Silver Limes (maa_009) and Tulip Trees (maa_010) of Nolenspark, all within about 100 metres.
verify_notes: A group of three London planes the register dates to 1880-1890 (roughly 136-146 years old in 2026), planted during the westward 1886 expansion of Stadspark into Mgr. Nolenspark and Henri Hermanspark, per the register's own history note echoed independently by the general Stadspark/park-history record. This is a distinct cluster from the already-published 'Tallest Plane Tree in the Netherlands' (maa_005), which stands roughly 240 m away in a different part of the park system with no recorded age; these three planes are a separate, smaller, dated stand. Could not find a source naming this specific trio beyond the register; delivered flagged on that single-source basis. No girth recorded in this register's schema for this entry. Cheap density addition to the already-dense, already-published Nolenspark walk (4 trees within 100 m before this one).
